The access list for North Window Studio is kept in a blue binder beside the entrance, with a matching copy in the building manager’s office. It covers the print room, the small recording booth, and the shared worktable, but not the locked cabinet used by the ceramics group. The binder is updated when a member joins, changes their usual hours, or returns a key. At the monthly meeting on 14 March, members agreed to keep the list organized by room rather than by surname. That makes it easier to check who can enter a particular space without passing around everyone’s contact details. Each entry includes a member’s name, the room or rooms they may use, and any hours that differ from the regular schedule. Phone numbers remain on a separate emergency sheet in the manager’s office. A person’s access is not changed just because they stop attending meetings; Mara asks them directly whether they still need it.

The entrance sheet has a short note explaining that a listed name does not unlock every door. The outer entrance uses a fob, and individual rooms may have separate keys or codes. “I can let you into the building, but I can’t promise the print room is ready,” Luis said when a new member asked about evening access. His distinction has helped prevent confusion during events, when visitors sometimes assume the shared entrance fob also opens equipment rooms. Members are asked not to lend their fobs, even to another cooperative member, because the entry log records the assigned holder.

Mara corrected the paper record after checking the envelope, and Luis asked the building office to compare the fob number with its electronic register. The cooperative has not decided whether to move the binder to a wall-mounted holder, since members use the entrance area for deliveries and there is limited space. I signed the receipt after checking the last carton. The driver tucked a copy under the bakery’s noticeboard, and I moved the ceramics onto the shelves so the staff could unpack them after the morning rush.

Mara stored the master video and caption files in separate folders, with matching filenames so that staff could locate them without opening each document. The archive planned to show the concert during its winter program, but the file itself was also intended for online access. Eli kept a copy of the approved version alongside the earlier draft, preserving the review history and the original timecodes for the uncertain balcony comment.
